content_metadata.description: A reflective interview with Vivian Campbell discussing his experiences with Ronnie James Dio, including compensation promises, challenges with management, and his journey towards accepting his legacy with the band.

qAndA.answer: Vivian Campbell is playing a silver Gibson Les Paul electric guitar.
qAndA.question: What type of guitar is Vivian Campbell playing throughout the video?

qAndA.answer: Vivian Campbell describes it as a modest wage for the first three albums in exchange for no participation in album sales, tour receipts, merchandise money, or any other revenue.
qAndA.question: How does Vivian Campbell describe the initial agreement with Ronnie regarding compensation?

qAndA.answer: Ronnie promised to make it an equity situation by the third album, where the band members would get part of the record sales and tour revenue.
qAndA.question: What was the specific promise Ronnie made regarding compensation?

qAndA.answer: Vivian Campbell suggests it was Wendy Dio, Ronnie's ex-wife and manager, who was not present when the original promise was made.
qAndA.question: Who does Vivian Campbell suggest was the primary reason for Ronnie not honoring his promise?

qAndA.answer: Vivian Campbell has come to fully embrace his legacy with Dio and feels proud of the music they created together. It took him a long time to reach this point due to the pain of his firing, but Ronnie's passing allowed him to see the situation in a different light.
qAndA.question: How does Vivian Campbell feel about his time with Dio now?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Okay, so you mentioned about being fired from the Osband.
You mentioned you didn't leave, you were fired.
So how did that go down?
Well, when the band was first formed, Ronnie told Zinni and Jimmy and myself that for the
first three records, if we were willing to not be participants in the album sales or
the tour receipts or the merchandise money or any of that, if we were willing to work
for a very modest wage that by the third album he would make an equity situation and we
would get part of the record and part of the tours, etc.
So we worked for Lesson the Road crew.
I mean, we did the Holy Diver album, we got paid $100 a week.
When we started the Holy Diver tour, our pay was bumped up to $400 a week and so on over
the years, over the Holy Diver tour and the last line tour and the Sacred Heart tour.
And our wages were gradually increased from tour to tour.
We were getting paid less than our lighting designer, for example, and things we got in
and but we were also writing the songs with Ronnie.
We were part of the creative process, but we got no, none of the record sales.
We got none of the merchandise money and none of the content money.
So we were, we were okay with that because Ronnie had promised us that by the third album
that would all change.
We were working towards this goal and the band was becoming more and more successful.
And when the third album came along, I was the first one to say to Ronnie to remind him
of the promise that he made us back in 1982 when the band was formed before we did Holy
Diver record.
And I brought it up to Ronnie when we were recording the third album, Sacred Heart and Ronnie
said, let's get through the record first and then we'll discuss it.
So I waited until the record was done and then I brought it up again.
And Ronnie said, well, let's get on the road and get rehearsed.
And once the tour starts, we can discuss it with Wendy.
Wendy was his ex-wife and manager of the band, his manager.
And with Banner sort of hindsight, I see it very clearly now.
It really came down to this.
There were only four people in the room when Ronnie made that promise.
And that was Ronnie and Jimmy and Vinnie and myself.
Wendy deal wasn't in the room.
And Ronnie really never stood up to his ex-wife and he never had the courage to tell her that
he had made this promise to us.
And she never saw the value in the original band.
She was only, I think so creatively shortsighted that she could only see that it was Ronnie.
He didn't see value in who played on stage with Ronnie or who wrote songs with Ronnie.
She just thought that everyone could be replaced.
Whereas I think Ronnie really realized the chemistry that the original band had and he
really valued that.
But when it came down to it, he didn't have the courage to stand up to Wendy and he figured
that it was easier to just get rid of me.
And that's what he did.
So it was, you know, people can say it's about money.
And yes, in black and white terms, it is about money.
But more importantly to me is that it was about principle.
I believe strongly in principle.
I always have, I believe in integrity in people.
And when I look someone in the eye and I shake their hand and I make a deal with them,
I will uphold my hand of the deal and I expect the same of other people.
And Ronnie didn't do that for me.
So that's why I was fired from the band and it left such a bad taste in my mouth for
so many years.
I was so hurt by the whole process that after that, you know, I didn't make the mistake
of saying very hurtful things about Ronnie and the press.
As indeed, he said to Sam about me, I think that was a mistake for both of us to do that.
It was a very painful thing for me because I never wanted to leave that band.
I was fully invested in it.
I enjoyed it immensely.
I believed in it and I give blood, sweat and tears and everything I had creatively
over the course of three albums to build that band.
And then to be unceremoniously dumped like that was very, very painful for me.
So it took me a long time to come full circle.
To be honest, I think it all took Ronnie's passing for me to be able to look at that in a different light.
And you know, realized that it was as much Jimmy Banseridage and Vinnie Apathy's
heritage and my heritage as it was Ronnie's and we all owned those records and that history.
And so now I've come to fully embrace it.
Whereas for many, many years, it was too painful for me to even listen to it.
But came on the radio, I would turn the radio off.
I didn't own any of the records.
I wanted nothing to do with it.
And now I sit in an entirely different light.
I realized that we own it as much as Ronnie.
And that it's a joyous thing to embrace.
And it makes me incredibly happy to be on stage with Vinnie and with Jimmy Wiley with life
and to play that music again, you know.
It's something I'm very, very, very proud of.
But it took me a long time to get here.
And that's the reason why.
